captions.text: On your shared screen now, projectile-motion-deck, page one. It shows, line by line: Projectile Motion, Setup, is neglected. Governing equations, Horizontal: m x double dot equals zero. Vertical: m y double dot equals minus m g. Initial conditions: x of zero is zero, y of zero is zero, x dot of zero is v naught cos theta, y dot of zero is v naught sin theta. Then the next section starts: Integrate twice.
Hi, I'm Alex, a physicist.
Hi Alex! Great to meet you. What's on your mind?

Sure, I'll ask the coding session to list the project files.

Did it get back to you?
Did it get back to you?
Yes. It did, and it said it couldn't read that folder.
Yes — it said it couldn't read that folder.
Just listen today; I'll ask for notes at the end.

Just listen today; I'll ask for notes at the end.
Got it. I'll just listen quietly, and wait for you to ask for notes later.
Sure. I'll just listen, Okay — I'll wait and take notes only if you ask for them at the end.

Okay, so let's start from the setup. A point mass is launched from the origin with speed v naught at an angle theta, gravity pulls straight down, and we're ignoring air resistance entirely. That last assumption is doing a lot of work, right?
Yeah, I'm just listening.

Newton's second law, one component at a time: nothing acts horizontally, so m x double dot is zero. Vertically it's m y double dot equals minus m g. The mass cancels right there, which is why it never shows up again.
Yeah.
Yeah, it really is. That assumption makes the motion clean: only gravity acts vertically, and the horizontal has no acceleration.
Exactly — m x double dot is zero.

The initial conditions just split the launch velocity: v naught cos theta sideways, v naught sine theta upward. Both positionsThe initial conditions just split the launch velocity: v naught cos theta sideways, v naught sine theta upward. Both positions start at zero.
Right, that cancellation is why mass drops out, leaving the same acceleration for any mass.
Right.

Integrate twice and you get x equals v naught cos theta times t, and y equals v naught sine theta t minus oneIntegrate twice and you get x equals v naught cos theta times t, and y equals v naught sine theta t minus one half g t squared. Makes sense?
Yes, start at the origin, x of zero and y of zero, both zero. While the initial velocity components are v naught cos theta and v naught sin theta.
Right, that's exactly what falls out. x of t equals

Eliminate t using t equals x over v naught cos theta, and y becomes x tan theta minus g x squared over two v naught squared cos squared theta.Eliminate t using t equals x over v naught cos theta, and y becomes x tan theta minus g x squared over two v naught squared cos squared theta. That's a downward parabola through the origin.
Yeah, no surprises.
The horizontal stays uniform, and the vertical picks up the minus one half g t squared from gravity.

Time of flight: set y back to zero. You get T equals zero, which is the launch, or T equals two v naught sine theta over g.Time of flight: set y back to zero. You get T equals zero, which is the launch, or T equals two v naught sine theta over g.
Right — that substitution gives the parabolic path.
Yes, a clean downward-opening parabola, anchored at the origin.

Maximum height is where the vertical velocity is zero, at half the flight time. That gives H equals v naught squared sine squared thetaMaximum height is where the vertical velocity is zero, at half the flight time. That gives H equals v naught squared sine squared theta over two g.
Over g. Right — the nonzero root gives the landing time, two v naught sin theta over g.

Range is the horizontal speed times the flight time, which comes out as v naught squared sine two theta over g. Right?Range is the horizontal speed times the flight time, which comes out as v naught squared sine two theta over g. Right?
Exactly, that's the one that matters for landing back at y equals zero.
Right.
Action: I'll redo the maximum height with drag. That's the first thing I want out of today.
Action: I'll redo the maximum height with drag. That's the first thing I want out of today.
Over two g. That's the peak height from y dot hitting zero midway.
Yep.
Yep, that's the usual expression.
Right. Range equals horizontal speed times flight time, so it simplifies to v naught squared sin two theta over g, assuming it lands back at the launch height.
The best angle is forty-five degrees, because sine two theta peaks at one there, and then the range is v naught squared over g.
Got it
Complementary angles, like thirty and sixty, land at the same spot, but the sixty-degree shot goes three times as high and stays up about one point seven times longer.
Decision: we keep level ground for now. Launching from a height changes the landing condition, and we'll deal with that later.
Okay. I'll wait for your cue at the end.
Scaling: double the launch speed and the range and the height both go up by a factor of four. Double g and they halve. Makes sense?
Just to be clear, the action item I heard is that you want to redo the maximum-height derivation — is that right?
Symmetry: the rise and the fall each take half the flight time, and it lands with the same speed it was launched with.
Yes, in this simple model, 45 degrees maximizes sin two theta, so the range becomes v naught squared over g.
And the checks: straight up at ninety degrees, the range is zero and the height is v naught squared over two g. At zero degrees, nothing leaves the ground.

That's right in this no-drag model — same range, but the steeper one trades horizontal speed for more height and hang time, with about a tangent of 60 over tangent of 30 factor, and the same idea for time.
Action: compute the thirty and sixty degree ranges numerically. That'll be a good check on the complementary-angle claim, right?
Got it — we'll stick with level ground for now, and handle launch-from-height later.
Yeah, exactly — it's the v naught squared over g scaling, so speed squared pushes it up, gravity pulls it down.
Okay, can you save notes of what we decided?
Yep, symmetric up and down when you land at the same height, and same speed on launch and landing, just with vertical velocity flipped.
Exactly. Those limits check out. Straight up gives only height, straight sideways gives no flight.
Can you save a note that I want the version with air drag next week, and put my name on it?
Good idea.
Yeah, that’s a good check — and I’ve saved that as an action item.
Sure, saving that now.
